proposals.impact: reduce zero-start drop-off on quiz intro screen
proposals.observation: The quiz had 1 session in the last 48 hours. That session loaded the intro screen and went no further: starts = 0, completions = 0, furthest_step_distribution shows only "intro_load": 1. The single visitor arrived via direct traffic, which suggests they already knew about the quiz (possibly Joel himself, possibly a warm referral) yet still did not press start. The intro screen is the only friction point in the data. Nothing else explains a 100% drop at the first interaction.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the quiz intro screen's headline and subhead. The current text (see CURRENT_TEXT) is generic enough that a visitor who arrives already curious can still feel uncertain about what they are walking into. The Sultanic test fails it: any 1,000 coaches could have written it. Replace with copy that names the specific feeling the ICP carries into the page, using concrete language rooted in Joel's observed client reality rather than category-level framing. No structural changes to the file, no new components. One text swap.

proposals.impact: lift Money Worship open rate closer to Vigilance benchmark
proposals.observation: Money Vigilance automation: 66.67% open rate on 12 sends. Money Worship automation: 37.5% open rate on 16 sends. That is a 29-percentage-point gap between two sequences running inside the same list, same sender name, same sending infrastructure. The difference is almost certainly the subject line and preview text, not list quality or send time, because both sequences share the same origin funnel. Lifting Worship even halfway toward Vigilance's rate would meaningfully improve downstream coaching enquiries from that segment.
proposals.proposal: Rewrite the subject line (and preview text if present) of email 1 in the Money Worship sequence. The word "worship" in behavioural-money research describes people who over-attach meaning and security to accumulation. The ICP in this segment earns well but feels quietly ashamed of how much they think about money, or how little the number in their account seems to change their anxiety. The subject line should name that lived tension rather than label the archetype. One file, one field edit.

proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why do I check my bank balance ten times a day but still feel like I have no idea where I stand?"
pubDate: "2026-07-27"
draft: true
---

There is a specific version of this. You open the app before coffee. You open it again after lunch, not because anything has changed but because maybe the number will feel different this time, or maybe you are checking that it hasn't quietly dropped. By the evening you have looked four or five more times. You know the balance. You have always known the balance. The checking is not about information.

Joel sees this with a lot of clients who earn well and spend carefully. The behaviour looks like diligence from the outside. From the inside it feels closer to low-level dread with a refresh button.

What the checking is actually doing is trying to resolve a feeling that account data cannot resolve. The number goes up, the checking continues. The number is fine, the dread stays. That pattern has a name in behavioural research, and it predates whatever salary you are on now.

If you recognise that loop, the quiz below takes four minutes. It won't diagnose you. It will show you which pattern is most likely driving the behaviour, in plain language, with no obligation attached.
